title: Rented Junior Risk Capital can be used to compel a counterparty into revenue sharing
content:
A.2.8.2.1.2.1.1 states the term precisely: "Each Agent retains the right to force the other Prime Agent to do revenue sharing up to 40% by providing that Prime with rented JRC. Sharing is done on the net revenue after deducting the cost to Sky. This is only considered on the spread earned on USDS debt, including any subsidy amounts."

The striking word is *force*. This is not an option to negotiate a share — it is a unilateral right exercised by supplying something the counterparty may not have asked for. Providing junior risk capital automatically buys a claim on up to 40% of the resulting spread.

The economic logic holds together. Junior capital is the tranche that absorbs losses first, so a Prime supplying it is genuinely taking risk on the other's positions, and a revenue claim is the natural compensation. Making the right unilateral prevents the recipient from refusing capital in order to keep all upside while relying on the ecosystem to absorb a failure.

The base is carefully bounded: only "the spread earned on USDS debt, including any subsidy amounts," net of Sky's cost. Sharing therefore applies to the margin on borrowed liquidity — the return most directly attributable to the capital structure supporting it — and "including any subsidy amounts" pulls subsidised borrowing into the shared pool, so a Prime cannot keep concessionary funding benefits to itself while sharing only the market-rate portion.

What the provision leaves open is pricing. Nothing states how much JRC buys how much share up to the 40% ceiling, which makes the term a framework for a negotiation whose outcome the ceiling merely caps.
description: Under Ecosystem Accord 1 each of Grove and Spark may force the other into a revenue share of up to 40% by supplying it with rented JRC, computed on the USDS debt spread net of Sky's cost.
